caught.text: Oh! Hi! You caught me reading.

about.text: I'm a stick figure, I wear glasses, and I collect questions.

drop.text: People drop in the things they wonder about, and I go and find the answers.

today.text: Today, every answer is going to sound completely made up.

promise.text: But I promise, every single one is true.

ready.text: Ready? Let's pull out the first one.

closer.text: Ooh, good one. Let's take a closer look.

white.text: Sunlight looks white, but it's actually every colour mixed together.

colours.text: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, all travelling as one.

crash.text: To reach your eyes, that light has to crash through the air.

molecules.text: And air is packed with tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen.

trick.text: Here's the trick. Those molecules bounce blue light around much more than red light.

red.text: Red light has long, lazy waves. It mostly slips straight past.

blue.text: Blue light has short, choppy waves, and it gets knocked all over the sky.

everywhere.text: So wherever you look up, blue light is coming at you from every direction.

glows.text: That's why the whole sky glows blue!

violet.text: But wait. Violet waves are even shorter. So why isn't the sky purple?

less.text: The Sun sends us less violet, and our eyes just aren't very good at seeing it.

sunset.text: And at sunset, sunlight has to travel through much more air to reach you.

scatter.text: Most of the blue gets scattered away on the journey, leaving the reds and oranges.

painted.text: So the sky isn't painted blue. It's sunlight, bouncing around.

q.text: Next question! Is it true that octopuses have three hearts?

yes.text: Yes! Three hearts. I only have one, and honestly, I'm a little jealous.

gills.text: Two small hearts pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen.

body.text: The big third heart pumps that blood around the rest of the body.

weird.text: And here's the weird part. When an octopus swims, that big heart stops beating.

crawl.text: Swimming is exhausting! That's why octopuses would usually rather crawl.

blood.text: Oh, and their blood is blue.

iron.text: Our blood uses iron to carry oxygen, and that makes it red.

copper.text: Octopus blood uses copper instead, and that turns it blue.

brain.text: Plus, most of an octopus's brain cells aren't in its head. They're in its arms!

arms.text: Each arm can touch, taste, and make little decisions all by itself.

alien.text: Three hearts, blue blood, and thinking arms. Basically an alien. But real.

q.text: Ooh, this one's a classic. Is a banana a berry?

botanist.text: To a botanist, a berry is a fruit that grows from one flower with a single ovary.

inside.text: And its seeds are tucked inside the soft, squishy part.

fit.text: Bananas fit perfectly. See those tiny dark specks in the middle?

seeds.text: Those are seeds that never grew up.

yes.text: So yes. A banana is a berry!

club.text: And so are grapes, tomatoes, kiwis, and even eggplants.

straw.text: But strawberries? Not berries at all.

outside.text: A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside.

fruit.text: And each of those little seeds is actually its own tiny fruit.

lying.text: So the berry aisle is lying to you. The banana aisle is not.

q.text: Next! Does honey really never go bad?

tombs.text: Archaeologists exploring ancient Egyptian tombs found jars of honey thousands of years old.

how.text: So how does honey pull that off? Three tricks.

sugar.text: Trick one. Honey is mostly sugar, with very little water.

germs.text: Any germ that lands in it gets the water sucked right out of it. It shrivels up and gives up.

acid.text: Trick two. Honey is acidic, about as acidic as orange juice. Germs hate that.

enzyme.text: Trick three. Bees add a special enzyme.

peroxide.text: When honey gets a tiny bit wet, it makes a little hydrogen peroxide. Germ zapper!

lid.text: Just keep the lid on. If honey soaks up too much water, it can start to ferment.

crystals.text: And if your honey turns cloudy and crunchy, it hasn't gone bad. It's just crystals.

warm.text: Warm it up gently, and it melts right back.

q.text: Here's one about you. Are you taller in the morning?

yes.text: You are! By about a centimetre. Sometimes more.

spine.text: Your spine is a stack of bones, with squishy cushions in between, called discs.

gravity.text: All day long, gravity squashes you down.

squeeze.text: Walking, sitting, standing. Your discs get squeezed and lose a little water.

night.text: Then at night, you lie down flat. The pressure's off.

sponge.text: And your discs soak water back up, like little sponges.

wake.text: So you wake up a tiny bit taller, and shrink back down by dinner.

astro.text: Astronauts take this to the extreme.

space.text: With no gravity squashing them in space, they can grow up to three percent taller!

me.text: Me? I'm a stick figure. I'm exactly as tall as whoever draws me.

q.text: Last question in the jar. Is a day on Venus really longer than its year?

space.text: We need space for this one.

day.text: A day is how long a planet takes to spin around once.

year.text: A year is how long it takes to travel all the way around the Sun.

earth.text: Earth spins once a day, and circles the Sun in three hundred and sixty five days.

slow.text: Venus spins incredibly slowly. One turn takes two hundred and forty three Earth days.

zips.text: But it zips around the Sun in just two hundred and twenty five.

finish.text: So yes! Venus finishes a whole year before it finishes a single spin.

west.text: It even spins backwards compared to Earth, so on Venus, the Sun rises in the west.

lead.text: Just don't visit. The surface is hot enough to melt lead.

empty.text: And that's the whole jar! Empty.

recap1.text: The sky is scattered sunlight. Octopuses have three hearts. Bananas are berries.

recap2.text: Honey lasts for thousands of years, you're taller in the morning, and a day on Venus outlasts its year.

next.text: It says: What will you wonder about next?

bye.text: Drop it in the jar. I'll see you next time!
